name: The limits of humanist reform in the face of religious polarization
plain_explanation: Erasmus and More were suited to a moderate, reform-minded age that still allowed criticism of Church abuses without demanding a complete break from Rome; once Luther's revolt forced everyone to choose a side, their kind of moderate, humane, skeptical-but-pious temperament became untenable, and each was destroyed or neutralized by the more extreme age that followed.
precise_definition: Russell's diagnosis: 'Before Luther's revolt, they were leaders of thought, but after it the world was too violent, on both sides, for men of their type. More suffered martyrdom, and Erasmus sank into ineffectiveness... For honest men, the only honourable alternatives were martyrdom or victory... [Erasmus] lived too long, into an age of new virtues and new vices -- heroism and intolerance -- neither of which he could acquire.'
why_it_mattered: Explains the tragic arc of both men's later lives and offers a general pattern (moderate reformers overtaken by polarizing revolution) that Russell implicitly generalizes beyond the Reformation itself.
historical_origin: Precipitated specifically by Luther's 1517 revolt and, for Erasmus, by the 1524 free-will controversy.
examples: Erasmus's comment on More's martyrdom: 'Would More had never meddled with that dangerous business, and left the theological cause to the theologians'
More's execution in 1535 for refusing the Oath of Supremacy
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly tied to the Reformation's forced choice between Catholic and Protestant allegiance.
